title: The two-drop cliff
hook: Add base drop by drop. Does the pH climb steadily?

knows: that pH is a log scale: each unit is 10 times the H⁺
doesNotKnow: that near the equivalence point a few drops swing the pH by many units

misconception: pH changes in proportion to the base added.
objective: The learner can explain that titrating 25.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L HCl with 0.100 mol/L NaOH barely moves the pH for 24.9 mL, then 4 drops (24.9 to 25.1 mL) jump it from about 3.7 to 10.3, because pH counts powers of ten and the acid runs out exactly at 25.0 mL.

claims.text: At 24.90 mL of base the pH is about 3.7, and at 25.10 mL about 10.3: a jump of about 6.6 units.
claims.source: Strong acid/strong base, 25 °C, pKw 14.00. 24.90 mL: (2.500 − 2.490) × 10⁻³ mol H⁺ in 49.90 mL = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L → pH 3.70. 25.10 mL: 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol OH⁻ in 50.10 mL → pOH 3.70, pH 10.30. Node script; Demo.tsx pH().

claims.text: 0.2 mL is about 4 drops (one drop about 0.05 mL).
claims.source: A standard drop from a burette is about 0.05 mL (Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. on titration; European Pharmacopoeia 2.1.1 normalised dropper: 20 drops of water ≈ 1.0 g).

claims.text: The first 24.90 mL of base moves the pH only about 2.7 units (from 1.0).
At 24.90 mL only 1 part in 250 of the acid is left, still about 2 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L of H⁺.
The steep rise sits at the equivalence point, where acid and base match, which is why titrations find it so sharply.
claims.source: Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, 'titration curves'; Skoog et al., Fundamentals of Analytical Chemistry.

recall.question: Halfway through titrating a strong acid with a strong base, you have added half the base needed. Is the pH near 7?
recall.why: Half the acid is still there; on a log scale that is barely a change. The pH only shoots up in the last drops at the match.
